chapterNote: James, the Lord's brother, writes the New Testament's book of wisdom — Proverbs for the church — to Jewish believers scattered across the empire, and he opens at full speed. Count trials as joy, because tested faith works endurance and endurance matures a man toward completeness. Ask God for wisdom and ask undivided, for the double-souled man is a wave the wind owns. Poverty and riches are both leveled by the flower-fading brevity of life. Then the chapter's careful anatomy of temptation: God tests but never tempts; each man is dragged off and baited by his own desire, and desire conceives sin, and sin full-grown gives birth to death — while every good and perfect gift keeps coming down from the Father of lights, in whom there is no shifting shadow at all. The closing charge sets the book's whole agenda: be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; be doers of the word and not self-deceived hearers who forget their own face in the mirror; and know that religion God calls pure has hands and feet — orphans and widows visited, and a life kept unstained from the world.

1.text: James, a slave of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes scattered abroad in the Dispersion: greetings.
1.amp: James [Iakobos, the Lord's brother], a servant [doulos — a bond-slave] of God [theos] and of the Lord [kurios] Jesus [Iesous] Christ [Christos — Messiah, Anointed One], to the twelve [dodeka] tribes which are scattered abroad [diaspora — the Dispersion], greeting [chairein].
1.notes: The doulos (G1401), the bond-slave: the Lord's own brother claims no family rank, only ownership. The diaspora (G1290) is the scattering of Israel among the nations — believing Jews far from home, for whom trial was the weather. His greeting chairein (G5463) puns straight into verse 2's chara, joy.

2.text: My brothers, count it nothing but joy whenever you fall into trials of every kind,
2.amp: My brethren [adelphos], count it [hegeomai — reckon it, weigh it out and conclude] all [pas] joy [chara] when you fall into [peripipto — fall in among, as among robbers] divers temptations ['trials', the KJV margin — peirasmos];
2.notes: hegeomai (G2233) is a deliberate act of accounting, not a feeling. peirasmos (G3986) covers both trial and temptation — the same pressure, read from God's side or the enemy's. The falling-word (G4045) is the one used of the traveler who fell among thieves (cf. Luke 10:30): trials ambush.

3.text: because you know this: the proving of your faith works endurance.
3.amp: Knowing [ginosko] this, that the trying [dokimion — the testing that proves genuineness] of your faith [pistis] works [katergazomai — works out, produces] patience [hupomone — endurance, the strength to remain under].
3.notes: dokimion (G1383) is the assayer's word: the test that proves the metal real. hupomone (G5281) is literally 'remaining under' — not gritted teeth but load-bearing strength, and it is manufactured (katergazomai, G2716) by nothing except tested pistis (G4102).

4.text: And let endurance finish its perfect work, so that you may be mature and whole, lacking in nothing.
4.amp: But let patience [hupomone] have her perfect [teleios — complete, mature] work [ergon], that you may be perfect [teleios] and entire [holokleros — whole in every part], wanting [leipo — lacking, falling short in] nothing.
4.notes: teleios (G5046) is completeness of growth, maturity rather than sinlessness. The danger is aborting the process — praying the trial away before its ergon (G2041) is done. holokleros (G3648): whole with every part intact, nothing of the man left undeveloped.

5.text: If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives to everyone generously and without scolding, and it will be given him.
5.amp: If any of you lack [leipo] wisdom [sophia], let him ask [aiteo] of God [theos], that gives [didomi] to all [pas] men liberally [haplos — simply, generously, with a single undivided intent], and upbraids [oneidizo — reproaches, scolds] not; and it shall be given him.
5.notes: The lack-word leipo (G3007) repeats from verse 4: the one shortage with a standing remedy. haplos (G574) is single-handed giving, no strings and no hesitation, and God never oneidizo (G3679), never rubs the asker's nose in his need. Wisdom here is skill for trials, Proverbs-wisdom, and it comes by aiteo (G154), plain asking.

6.text: But let him ask in faith, with no doubting in him, for the doubter is like a wave of the sea, wind-driven and tossed about.
6.amp: But let him ask [aiteo] in faith [pistis], nothing wavering [diakrino — divided in judgment, disputing with oneself]. For he that wavers is like [eiko] a wave [kludon] of the sea [thalassa], driven with the wind [anemizo] and tossed [rhipizo].
6.notes: diakrino (G1252) is to be at odds with yourself, the inner debate that asks while half-expecting nothing. The kludon (G2830) is the surge of open water: no shape of its own, all its motion borrowed from the last wind (anemizo, G416) that crossed it.

7.text: That man should not suppose he will receive anything from the Lord;
7.amp: For let not that [ekeinos] man [anthropos] think [oiomai] that he shall receive [lambano] any thing of the Lord [kurios].
7.notes: Not because God grew stingy between verses — the giving of verse 5 stands — but because the divided asker has no hands still enough to lambano (G2983), to take hold of what is handed him.

8.text: he is a double-souled man, unstable in all his ways.
8.amp: A double minded [dipsuchos — double-souled, two-souled] man [aner] is unstable [akatastatos — unsettled, restless] in all [pas] his ways [hodos].
8.notes: dipsuchos (G1374), a word James may have coined: one man carrying two souls that want different things. akatastatos (G182) is the instability that follows him everywhere — not just at prayer but in pas hodos (G3956, G3598), every road he takes.

9.text: Let the brother of humble means glory in his high position,
9.amp: Let the brother [adelphos] of low degree [tapeinos — humble, lowly] rejoice ['glory', kauchaomai, the KJV margin — boast, exult] in that he is exalted [hupsos — his height, his high station]:
9.notes: kauchaomai (G2744) is boasting-language, deliberately scandalous: the poor believer has actual rank to boast in — son of God, heir of the kingdom (cf. 2:5) — and the low seat at the world's table changes none of it.

10.text: and the rich brother in his being brought low, because like a flower of the field he will pass away.
10.amp: But the rich [plousios], in that he is made low [tapeinosis — his humbling]: because as the flower [anthos] of the grass [chortos] he shall pass away [parerchomai].
10.notes: The rich man's true boast is his tapeinosis (G5014), the humbling that faith teaches him before death teaches everyone: he is grass like the rest (cf. Isaiah 40:6-7). The anthos (G438) is the field-flower, glorious for a week.

11.text: For the sun rises with its scorching heat and withers the grass; its flower drops, and the beauty of its face is gone. Just so the rich man will wither away in the middle of his pursuits.
11.amp: For the sun [helios] is no sooner risen [anatello] with a burning heat [kauson — the scorching wind], but it withers [xeraino] the grass [chortos], and the flower [anthos] thereof falls [ekpipto], and the grace [euprepeia — the fair appearance] of the fashion of it perishes [apollumi]: so also shall the rich man [plousios] fade away [maraino] in his ways [poreia — his goings, his pursuits].
11.notes: The kauson (G2742) is the sirocco, the burning east wind that browns a hillside in a day. maraino (G3133), to fade like a bloom, and poreia (G4197), his business journeys: death finds the rich man mid-errand, calendar full.

12.text: Blessed is the man who endures under trial, for when he has been proved genuine he will receive the crown of life, which the Lord promised to those who love Him.
12.amp: Blessed [makarios] is the man [aner] that endures [hupomeno — remains under] temptation [peirasmos]: for when he is tried [dokimos — approved, proven genuine], he shall receive [lambano] the crown [stephanos — the victor's wreath] of life [zoe], which the Lord [kurios] has promised [epangello] to them that love [agapao] Him.
12.notes: The beatitude that crowns the trial-teaching: makarios (G3107), blessed, over the man still under the load. dokimos (G1384) is the assay-stamp on proven metal, and the stephanos (G4735) is the games-wreath — here woven of zoe (G2222), life itself. Love (agapao, G25), not achievement, names the heirs.

13.text: Let no one under temptation say, 'God is tempting me,' for God cannot be tempted by evil, and He Himself tempts no one.
13.amp: Let no man say [lego] when he is tempted [peirazo], 'I am tempted of God [theos]': for God cannot be tempted [apeirastos — untemptable] with evil [kakos], neither tempts He any man:
13.notes: The same peirazo (G3985) root as the trials of verse 2, but now in its dark sense: enticement toward sin. apeirastos (G551): God is unbaitable — evil has no hook that fits Him — and He baits no hooks Himself. The blame-shift is as old as Eden (cf. Genesis 3:12).

14.text: But each man is tempted when he is dragged off and baited by his own desire.
14.amp: But every man [hekastos] is tempted [peirazo], when he is drawn away [exelko — dragged out, lured off] of his own [idios] lust [epithumia — craving, strong desire], and enticed [deleazo — baited, as a fish with a lure].
14.notes: Two hunting-words: exelko (G1828), dragged from cover, and deleazo (G1185), taken with bait. The bait is custom-made — idios epithumia (G2398, G1939), his own desire — which is why no two men are caught on the same hook.

15.text: Then desire, once it has conceived, gives birth to sin; and sin, grown to full term, gives birth to death.
15.amp: Then when lust [epithumia] has conceived [sullambano], it brings forth [tikto — bears as a child] sin [hamartia]: and sin, when it is finished [apoteleo — come to full term], brings forth [apokueo — gives birth to] death [thanatos].
15.notes: A genealogy in one verse: epithumia conceives (G4815), bears hamartia (G266), and hamartia carried apoteleo (G658), to full term, delivers thanatos (G2288). Sin is never stillborn on its own; it must be refused at conception (cf. Romans 6:23).

16.text: Do not be led astray, my beloved brothers.
16.amp: Do not err [planao — be deceived, led wandering], my beloved [agapetos] brethren [adelphos].
16.notes: planao (G4105) is to wander off the road: the specific deception in view is verse 13's — believing God sends the bait. The warmth of agapetos (G27) softens nothing of the warning.

17.text: Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation, nor shadow cast by turning.
17.amp: Every good [agathos] gift [dosis — the act of giving] and every perfect [teleios] gift [dorema — the thing given] is from above [anothen], and comes down from the Father [pater] of lights [phos], with whom is no variableness [parallage — variation], neither shadow [aposkiasma] of turning [trope].
17.notes: Both the giving (dosis, G1394) and the gift (dorema, G1434) descend anothen (G509), from above. 'Father of lights' names the Maker of sun, moon, and stars — and unlike His lights, He has no parallage (G3883), no phases, no eclipse, no aposkiasma (G644), no shadow thrown by turning. The Giver is fixed noon.

18.text: By His own set will He gave us birth through the word of truth, so that we would be a kind of firstfruits of His creatures.
18.amp: Of His own will [boulomai — His deliberate purpose] begat He [apokueo — gave birth to] us with the word [logos] of truth [aletheia], that we should be a kind of firstfruits [aparche] of His creatures [ktisma].
18.notes: The same birth-verb as verse 15, apokueo (G616), set in deliberate contrast: desire births death; God births us. The instrument is the logos aletheia (G3056, G225), the word of truth, and the aparche (G536) is the first sheaf lifted to God as pledge of the whole harvest (cf. Leviticus 23:10).

19.text: So then, my beloved brothers, let every man be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger,
19.amp: Wherefore, my beloved [agapetos] brethren [adelphos], let every man [anthropos] be swift [tachus] to hear [akouo], slow [bradus] to speak [laleo], slow to wrath [orge]:
19.notes: Three speeds for one mouth and two ears: tachus (G5036) toward akouo (G191), bradus (G1021) twice over toward speech and orge (G3709). The proverb-shaped rule governs the whole letter — the tongue returns in force in chapter 3.

20.text: for the anger of man does not work the righteousness of God.
20.amp: For the wrath [orge] of man [aner] works [katergazomai] not the righteousness [dikaiosune] of God [theos].
20.notes: katergazomai (G2716), the producing-verb of verse 3 — what testing produces, temper cannot. Human orge may feel like zeal for justice in the moment; it simply does not manufacture dikaiosune (G1343), and James states it as flatly as a law of physics.

21.text: Therefore strip off all filthiness and the overflow of evil, and receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.
21.amp: Wherefore lay apart [apotithemi — strip off like soiled clothing] all filthiness [rhuparia] and superfluity [perisseia — the overflow] of naughtiness [kakia — malice, evil], and receive [dechomai — welcome] with meekness [prautes — gentleness, teachability] the engrafted [emphutos — implanted, rooted in] word [logos], which is able [dunamai] to save [sozo] your souls [psuche].
21.notes: apotithemi (G659) is the laundry-verb: sin as clothes to be stripped. The logos is emphutos (G1721), already planted at the new birth of verse 18 — the call is to welcome (dechomai, G1209) with prautes (G4240) what is already rooted, and let it grow to the sozo (G4982) of the psuche.

22.text: But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
22.amp: But be ye [ginomai] doers [poietes] of the word [logos], and not hearers [akroates] only, deceiving [paralogizomai — reasoning yourselves astray] your own selves [heautou].
22.notes: The akroates (G202) was the auditor who attended lectures with no intent to act. paralogizomai (G3884) is deception by miscalculation: the hearer's books show a credit for every sermon heard, and the audit of verse 25 will find nothing behind the entries. The theme verse of the whole letter.

23.text: For if anyone hears the word and does not do it, he is like a man studying in a mirror the face he was born with:
23.amp: For if any be a hearer [akroates] of the word [logos], and not a doer [poietes], he is like [eiko] unto a man [aner] beholding [katanoeo — observing carefully] his natural [genesis — the face of his birth] face in a glass [esoptron — a mirror]:
23.notes: katanoeo (G2657) is careful study, not a glance — the hearer genuinely looks. The esoptron (G2072) was polished bronze; the 'face of his genesis' (G1078) is the face he was born with, seen true for a moment.

24.text: he studies himself, walks away, and immediately forgets what sort of man he was.
24.amp: For he beholds [katanoeo] himself, and goes his way [aperchomai], and straightway [eutheos] forgets [epilanthanomai] what manner of man [hopoios] he was.
24.notes: Three verbs and a vanished image: looked, left, forgot. eutheos (G2112), immediately — the mirror's verdict does not survive the walk to the door. Hearing without doing has exactly this retention.

25.text: But the one who stoops to gaze into the perfect law of liberty and stays by it, becoming not a hearer who forgets but a doer who works, this man will be blessed in his doing.
25.amp: But whoso looks [parakupto — stoops down to gaze intently] into the perfect [teleios] law [nomos] of liberty [eleutheria — freedom], and continues [parameno — remains beside] therein, he being not a forgetful [epilesmone] hearer [akroates], but a doer [poietes] of the work [ergon], this man shall be blessed [makarios] in his deed [poiesis — his doing].
25.notes: parakupto (G3879) is the stooping-to-peer verb used of John at the empty tomb (cf. John 20:5): the opposite of the mirror-glance. The nomos of eleutheria (G3551, G1657) is God's word as the law that frees. parameno (G3887), to remain beside it — and the makarios lands not on the knowing but on the poiesis, the doing.

26.text: If anyone considers himself religious and yet does not bridle his tongue, he deceives his own heart, and his religion is worthless.
26.amp: If any man among you seem [dokeo — thinks himself] to be religious [threskos], and bridles [chalinagogeo — reins in as with a bit] not his tongue [glossa], but deceives [apatao] his own heart [kardia], this man's religion [threskeia — religious observance] is vain [mataios — empty, futile].
26.notes: threskeia (G2356) is the outward practice of religion, the observances. chalinagogeo (G5468), the bridle-verb, previews chapter 3's horse and bit: the unreined glossa (G1100) voids the whole account — mataios (G3152), the Septuagint's own word for the vapor of Ecclesiastes.

27.text: Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to look after orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unspotted from the world.
27.amp: Pure [katharos] religion [threskeia] and undefiled [amiantos — unstained] before [para] God [theos] and the Father [pater] is this, To visit [episkeptomai — look after, care for] the fatherless [orphanos] and widows [chera] in their affliction [thlipsis], and to keep [tereo — guard] himself unspotted [aspilos — without spot or blemish] from the world [kosmos].
27.notes: episkeptomai (G1980) is God's own visiting-word, care that shows up in person. Orphans and widows were the covenant's test-case for true worship (cf. Deuteronomy 10:18; Isaiah 1:17), and aspilos (G784) is the spotlessness of a sacrificial lamb: mercy toward the helpless and holiness against the kosmos (G2889), one religion, two hands.
